summary: Dallas psychiatrist James Grigson, nicknamed Dr. Death, testified in about 167 Texas capital trials from the late 1960s to the 1990s, often without examining defendants, assuring juries they would kill again and helping send innocent men to death row.

evidence.note: Grigson born January 1932 in Texarkana, Texas
begins testifying about capital defendants in 1967
Texas legislature creates future-dangerousness question for death sentences
1983 Supreme Court case upholds his diagnosis of a defendant he never examined
long segment on Randall Dale Adams, wrongly convicted and later exonerated
2004 study finds expert predictions of future violence almost always wrong
expelled from the APA in 1995 and the Texas psychiatric society in 1996
other junk forensic experts: hair comparison and falsified autopsies
both sides pay him retainers so the other side cannot hire him
dies of lung cancer in June 2004

notes: Part 1 spends about ten minutes on 19th-century forensic psychiatry (will contests, insanity law); treated as background, so covered_span starts at birth. The 2016 stay for Jeffrey Wood is a short coda, so reaches_present is false. Scope set to national because of the two US Supreme Court cases, though the harm is all in Texas; local is arguable. main_span ends at his 2004 death rather than the 1995 APA expulsion.
